subject: GPs on a sphere (again): simpler than we thought?

messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: GPs on a sphere (again): simpler than we thought?
parts:
Hi folks,

A while back, the list discussed the application of Gaussian Process modelling to a spherical topology (https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/z2hj0Zb1I6A/gFHK-BDhBpQJ) at which time it seemed that it was unsupported. I'm possibly (likely) being naive here, but after mulling it over I think that conclusion might be false. That is, Michael Betancourt's response was that placing and exploring a probability mass on a sphere is tricky, but so far as I understand it, that's not what we'd be doing in the case of a GP.

The probability mass explored by all GPs will necessarily be a multivariate Gaussian, and where the spherical bit comes in would be in the computation of the covariance matrix. In my prior thinking, I was erroneously thinking that having spherical data defined by lat/long put me in the "multivariate inputs" case (page 161 of manual version 2.9.0). I now realize that while the spherical data is indeed defined by two variables, what is important for any given pair of points is merely their great circle distance, thus reducing to the univariate case after all. (Note I also talked of including time as a variable, which would put things back in the multivariate inputs world again, time & space, but still just using great circle distance for the space dimension)

So, am I wrong here? Happy to be corrected, but excited to try this if I'm right!

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] GPs on a sphere (again): simpler than we thought?
parts:
Sort of.  Yes there is a distinguished distance function on the sphere (geodesic distance with respect to the unique flat metric on the sphere and the  Levi-Cevita connection), but that doesn't mean that you can just throw it into a squared exponential kernel.   You
still have to choose a kernel that is consistent with functions on the sphere and deal with any potential nonidentifiabilities.  

For a sine kernel I think this might be okay, but just remember that you'll only be able to make inferences relative to your data, not absolute on the sphere.  Ultimately the GP uses the data to anchor the coordinates and remove many of the problems, but only when making statements relative to those points.
